clue.text: Worthless son accepting stories I dismissed as unfounded

parts.note: base means low and of little value

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so the pair before this word wraps around what follows
a letter that is dismissed is sent away, so the named letter drops out of the word for stories

parts.note: untrue stories
taken as written
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A dismissive verdict on a son whose tales are written off as groundless.
explanation.walkthrough: Worthless and son form a pair together, and the shortened stories slot between them rather than inside either word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something baseless has no foundation in fact, so the two adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Following disgrace Athos regularly gets drunk

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the selected letters come after the word for disgrace

parts.note: a blot on one's record is a disgrace

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the name is kept

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of the musketeer's name

explanation.surface: After a scandal, one of the Three Musketeers drinks too much now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: Athos is one of Dumas's Three Musketeers, known for his drinking, which suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Blotto is British slang for very intoxicated, a synonym of drunk.

clue.text: Hard to be secretive over support

indicators.note: in a down clue over means covering on top and below, so the secretive word spreads around the support

parts.note: sly means furtive or secretive
a tee supports a golf ball

explanation.surface: It is difficult to keep quiet about backing someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Steely means hard like steel, in material or in manner.

clue.text: Find Joyce oddly failing to interrupt recently

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into, so the surviving letters go inside the word for recently

parts.note: lately or of late means recently

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters fail, so only the even-placed ones survive

parts.note: second and fourth letters of the name

explanation.surface: A search for Joyce, who has strangely been failing to interrupt lately.
explanation.definitionFit: To locate something is to find where it is, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Easiness of heartless spy holding captive without question

indicators.note: without a heart means the middle letter is removed from the word that follows
holding means gripping on both sides, so what is left wraps around the next word

parts.note: spy with its middle letter removed
implicit trust is trust without question

explanation.surface: How easily a cruel spy keeps a prisoner without interrogation.
explanation.walkthrough: Captive reads as the prisoner but only joins the parts; implicit trust is trust given without question.
explanation.definitionFit: Simplicity is the quality of being easy to do or understand, which is easiness.

clue.text: Rick suffering primarily from piles

parts.note: a rick is a haystack, a stack of hay

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of the word before is kept

parts.note: the first letter of suffering

explanation.surface: Someone called Rick is in discomfort, chiefly owing to haemorrhoids.
explanation.walkthrough: Rick looks like a man's name, but it is the farming word for a stack of hay or straw; piles is not the ailment but heaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Stacks and piles are both heaps of things laid one on another, so the plural nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Distorted representation of very arty set cavorting outside

indicators.note: outside means surrounding, so the mixed letters go round the abbreviation
cavorting is prancing about, so those letters jump into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
V is the abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: A twisted picture of a pretentious crowd dancing around.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled letters of arty and set form a shell around V, so very is not part of the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A travesty is a grotesque parody or mockery, a distorted representation of something.

clue.text: Lines in support of dog being mine

indicators.note: in a down clue a support sits underneath, so these letters come below the dog

parts.note: a collie is a sheepdog
RY is short for railway, a set of lines

explanation.surface: A dog lead or fence lines seem to be claimed as somebody's own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mine' looks like a possessive pronoun but is the noun, a pit.
explanation.definitionFit: A colliery is a coal mine together with its buildings.

clue.text: Careless hit-and-run

parts.note: to slap is to hit
to dash is to run

explanation.surface: A careless driver is involved in a hit-and-run accident.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphens make hit-and-run look like one term for the crime, but it splits into two verbs.
explanation.definitionFit: Slapdash describes work done hastily and carelessly, so it is a synonym.

clue.text: Draw near on account of earlier defeat

parts.note: as in arguing over money, meaning because of it
to come is to approach

explanation.surface: An instruction to approach, given because of some earlier defeat.
explanation.definitionFit: To overcome an opponent is to beat them, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Gangster bound to return with a Spanish dish

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way you came, so the letters of gangster and bound are read backwards

parts.note: Al Capone, the Chicago gangster
a bound is a leap

explanation.surface: A mobster is obliged to come back carrying a plate of Spanish food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound to return' reads as 'obliged to come back', but bound is a jump and return turns the whole thing round.
explanation.definitionFit: Paella is the rice dish from Valencia, cooked with saffron, seafood or meat.

clue.text: Unlikely story of tasteless articles featuring students and beer!

indicators.note: something featuring an item has it included within, so the word for cheap goods holds the students

parts.note: tat is cheap and tasteless goods
L is learner, a student driver; two of them for the plural
ale is beer

explanation.surface: A far-fetched tale about cheap tacky goods, student life and beer.
explanation.walkthrough: L is the learner plate on a British car, so learners or students are L.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall tale is an exaggerated account hard to believe, the idiom for an unlikely story.

clue.text: Bottom discovers what's involved in difficult situation

indicators.note: something involved in a thing is caught up inside it, so the query word sits within the predicament

parts.note: being in a bind is being in a fix
eh? is a way of saying what?

explanation.surface: Someone at the lowest point finds out what lies behind a tricky situation.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is read as 'is', so 'what is involved in' means the query word goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Behind is an informal word for the buttocks, which is what bottom means here.

clue.text: Electric indicator showing jockey weighing relatively little

parts.note: to jockey or pilot is to steer or guide
light means of little weight

explanation.surface: A light jockey stands out like a little lamp on a panel.
explanation.walkthrough: Jockey suggests the rider at a racecourse, which fits weighing little, but here it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilot light is a small electric lamp showing that a device is switched on.

clue.text: Kind of soldiers to ignore argument against crossing river of biblical texts

indicators.note: crossing is read as straddling, so the remaining letters lie on either side of the river
to ignore something is to leave it out, so that short word is dropped from the soldiers

parts.note: conscripts are soldiers called up compulsorily
a con is an argument against, as in pros and cons
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: Some soldiers are told to disregard objections while crossing a river mentioned in the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: The argument against comes off the front of the soldiers, and the Ure is a river in Yorkshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scriptures are the sacred writings of the Bible, so they are biblical texts.

clue.text: Her wiles endlessly intriguing after Cowley's earliest satirical verse

indicators.note: without an end means the last letter of that word is cut off
after means following, so the mixed letters come after the initial
earliest means first, so only the opening letter of the name is kept

parts.note: the first letter of Cowley

indicators.note: intriguing as plotting or scheming suggests the letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
wiles with its last letter removed

explanation.surface: A woman's tricks are fascinating, following a satirical poem by someone named Cowley.
explanation.walkthrough: A clerihew is a four-line comic biographical verse, named after its inventor Edmund Clerihew Bentley.
explanation.definitionFit: The clerihew is a humorous, often mocking, quatrain about a famous person, so it is a kind of satirical verse.

clue.text: Written reports of profit sharing at the outset

parts.note: the first letter of sharing

explanation.surface: Financial records showing how profits are divided from the very beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a company's books, which are also accounts, but the word is built from account in its old sense of profit.
explanation.definitionFit: Accounts are narratives or descriptions of events, so written ones are reports.

clue.text: Stick out for the original blue

parts.note: pro means in favour of

indicators.note: original means first, so only the opening letter of the article is used

parts.note: the first letter of the
blue jokes are rude ones

explanation.surface: Persevering with the first shade of blue.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue as in risqué or smutty, not the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: To protrude is to project beyond a surface, which is to stick out.

clue.text: Spike getting adequate amount of rent

parts.note: to spike a drink is to lace it with alcohol
a ration is a fixed allowance

explanation.surface: Someone called Spike collects a fair share of the rent money.
explanation.walkthrough: Rent looks like money paid to a landlord, but it is the noun for a tear, the past tense of rend.
explanation.definitionFit: A laceration is a tear in the flesh, and a rent is a tear or rip.

clue.text: Priest describing more than enough left out to spoil

explanation.surface: A priest says that leaving out too much would ruin things.
explanation.walkthrough: Describe is used in its geometry sense of drawing a line around something.
explanation.definitionFit: To pamper someone is to indulge them excessively, which is to spoil them.

clue.text: Extremely costly bit of gear to catch young bird

taken as written

clue.text: Home of Ethelred's wife it includes Tewkesbury essentially

indicators.note: includes means takes inside, so the pair wife and it has the core letters placed among them

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for wife
